newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-OPINION - INSIDE CANBERRA - Govt fails on unfair dismissals.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-OPINION - INSIDE CANBERRA - Govt fails on unfair dismissals.

text.p: We said (on November 8) in commenting on the government's proposed new unfair dismissals law: "In short, there will be no great diminution of worry for the boss in sacking an employee under the Howard law than under the Brereton legislation."
Following passage of the government's industrial relations legislation in the Senate this week we can now confirm the accuracy of what we predicted on unfair dismissals.

As Labor's Deputy Senate Leader, Senator Nick Sherry, said in the committee stages on Monday: "There are going to be a lot of disappointed people out there who thought the Prime Minister, Mr Howard, was going to abolish the unfair dismissal laws."

And he further said: "The most fundamental point about the government's amendments to our unfair dismissal law is that the substance of the law -- the substantive provisions which will be applied in determining whether a dismissal was unfair -- is basically unchanged.
"Remember the hysteria about the so-called requirement for the employer to give the employee a warning before dismissal? Well, it is still there."
No government minister rose in the debate to rebut Senator Sherry's assertion.
Inside Canberra has already made the point that one change in the legislation is that all complaints of unfair dismissal must start with the Industrial Relations Commission.

A reading of Hansard reveals that Section 170CG of the Workplace Relations legislation requires the commission to consider whether there was a valid reason for the termination related to the conduct of the employee, whether the employee was notified of that reason and whether the employee was given an opportunity to respond to that reason.
But the matter does not end there.
The commission is then required "to conciliate" between the employer and employee over the disputed dismissal.
If the conciliation process is unsuccessful the matter must go to arbitration or a court, depending on the grounds on which the commission was asked to conciliate.
Not only that, the commission is required to consider whether the employee was "warned" about any unsatisfactory performance before getting the sack.
The Howard Government's legislation even preserves the Brereton maximum damages claim which can be awarded to an employee on grounds of unfair dismissal -- $32,000.
Senator Sherry said: "I have no doubt there will be many lawyers advising employers that they must still give an employee a warning before dismissal if they are not to fall foul of these laws."
Precisely.
John Howard hammered the unfair dismissal issue remorselessly in the campaign.
He undoubtedly left the small business sector believing it would be relatively easy and worry free to sack a no-hoper.
This will not be the case.
The new unfair dismissal law applies to all employees under Federal awards and employees of the Commonwealth and territories.
Most of the states have similar unfair dismissal laws for State awards to those which have just passed the Federal Parliament except Victoria.
However all Victorian employers will be caught by the new Federal laws when Jeff Kennett passes his IR powers over to the Commonwealth.
-- Inside Canberra 61-6 273-1600
